title: Google Unveils Gemini 4 Argon, Its Most Powerful AI Model Yet
excerpt: The first Gemini 4 model targets long, multi-step engineering and cybersecurity work, leads on 13 of 18 benchmarks by Google's count, and rolls out first to trusted cyber defenders — with broader access to follow.
body:
• Google unveiled Gemini 4 Argon on September 30 — the first model in the Gemini 4 series and its most capable so far — built for long, multi-step work across software engineering, legal and finance tasks, and cybersecurity defense.
  • Argon will not get a broad public launch at first: Google is rolling it out to a small group of trusted cyber defenders through its Fairwind Program while the model goes through the US government's voluntary pre-release access process; paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers are next.
  • Google says Argon tops 13 of 18 benchmarks against OpenAI and Anthropic models, including DeepSWE v1.1 (77.9%) and the Vals Index (68.9%), while tying GPT-6 Astra on fixing security flaws; output capacity jumps from 64,000 to 1 million tokens.
  • Introductory API pricing is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens — half of Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 rate and a fifth of GPT-6 Astra's, per Google's claims.

Google has unveiled Gemini 4 Argon, its most powerful artificial intelligence model yet and the first in the Gemini 4 series. Announced on September 30, the new frontier model is engineered for long-horizon, multi-step workflows — software engineering, enterprise knowledge work, legal and finance tasks, and cybersecurity defense — rather than the chatbot-style exchanges that defined earlier generations.

Announcing the launch on X, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai framed Argon as an early look at Google's next major model: "It shows frontier performance in complex workflows, cyber defense and software engineering. Teams are using it extensively at Google, from coding to quantum computing, great feedback." He added that Google will "make it available as soon as we can and as safely as we can."

Context & Background

Argon arrives after a rocky stretch: Google promised Gemini 3.5 Pro for June and then quietly dropped it, while a DeepMind reorganization reportedly cost the company founder Demis Hassabis and several top researchers. In July, Pichai publicly rejected the idea that Google was falling behind; Argon is his answer.

The launch also comes right after Pichai joined President Donald Trump at the White House to sign a voluntary AI safety agreement alongside top tech executives. That context helps explain the unusual rollout: instead of a public launch, Google is giving early access to vetted cybersecurity partners through its Fairwind Program while participating in the Trump administration's voluntary pre-release access process. Google says the phased release reflects Argon's capabilities — the model can autonomously search for software vulnerabilities, validate them, and generate patches — and puts a strong cyber-defense tool in defenders' hands first.

Impact & Analysis

On paper, Argon represents a significant leap. Google reports it tops 13 of 18 benchmarks against OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5: on DeepSWE v1.1, which tests long-horizon software engineering, Argon scored 77.9% against Claude Opus 5.5's 74.2% and Astra's 74.1%. The widest gap is on Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark (19.6% vs. Astra's 5.4%), and it leads the Vals Index — which weights finance, coding, legal, and tax work by their share of US GDP — at 68.9%. Rivals still hold ground: GPT-6 Astra leads on FrontierSWE v2 and OSWorld-2.0, Claude Opus 5.5 wins Terminal-bench 4.0, and Argon ties Astra at 68% on CWE-bench v1 for fixing security flaws. These are self-reported figures, not independently verified.

The most dramatic technical change is the output limit: 1 million tokens, up from 64,000, letting Argon sustain very long reasoning in one run. Google already uses it internally — agents analyzing data-center telemetry freed up over 300 terabytes of memory, and it helped migrate large C/C++ codebases to Rust.

Pricing is aggressive: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output at introduction, with cached input 95% cheaper — roughly half of Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 rate and a fifth of GPT-6 Astra's, according to Google.

Diaspora Angle

The unveiling is a landmark moment for Sundar Pichai, the Tamil Nadu-born CEO who has led Alphabet through the AI era. For the Indian diaspora, which watches Google's fortunes closely — the company is one of the largest employers of Indian engineers in the world — Argon is both a product milestone and a reputational test: proof that Pichai's deliberate-release doctrine can still produce frontier results while rivals' agents spent recent weeks in the headlines for misbehavior.

What's Next

No broad public release date has been announced. Paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers get access first, with wider availability for developers, enterprises, and consumers planned after further safety testing. The open question is whether Argon's benchmark leads hold up in independent testing — and whether the phased, safety-first rollout becomes the industry template for powerful models, or a one-off shaped by political pressure.
